label: 0057 · Smoothed in time, 1997–2025 (one QP over 53 windows): 0054 with a sheet 25 km below the Japan Trench interface after Tohoku and the interface's total coupling held to at most 1, uncorrelated noise, background coupling from −1 to 1, fourteen slow slip events as signal, fixed 747-site network, UNR positions (MAP)
description: Jack Loveless's proposal (issue #27): a sheet at the base of the subducting plate, the Japan Trench mesh moved 25 km straight down, for viscoelastic flow in the oceanic mantle after Tohoku. The sheet gets a Tohoku state of its own (strike- and dip-slip, either sense, one pattern, Omori with c = 1 yr). Unlike in 0054, the interface's total coupling, including its deficit state, is held to at most 1, so only the sheet can pull the forearc landward beyond full locking. The data see mostly the sum of the two: slip on the sheet correlates at −0.9 with slip on the interface at 0–20 km above it, and without the cap they run away in opposite senses (coupling 3.5 off Miyagi). With the cap, the interface off Miyagi at 0–20 km keeps slipping forward (410, 375 and 338 mm in 2011–12, 2012–16 and 2016–25; coupling 0.18 in 2012–2021, against 1.37 in 0054), and the sheet beneath it takes on 500–670 mm of slip deficit in each period. Seafloor residuals beneath the Japan Trench after Tohoku are 28 and 47 mm, and the onshore fit after Tohoku is 1.5% better than 0054's. Held-out data are predicted worse: seafloor cross-validation is +967 and onshore window cross-validation −5,330, against +1,138 and +548 for 0054, most of the loss in the first week after Tohoku. 0054 remains the preferred model. Seafloor data: Japan Coast Guard (CC BY-NC 4.0) and Tohoku University (CC BY 4.0).
